concepts.name: Sovereignty in detail: dependency, dominion, Commonwealth and the UN
concepts.description: India's status before and after 1947-50 and why Commonwealth and UN membership do not limit sovereignty.
concepts.idea: India moved from dependency to dominion to sovereign republic, and international memberships do not reduce sovereignty.
concepts.rule: Until the Independence Act 1947 India was a dependency (colony) of the British Empire. From 15 August 1947 to 26 January 1950 it was a dominion in the Commonwealth. It ceased to be a dominion on 26 January 1950 by declaring itself a sovereign republic; Pakistan remained a dominion until 1956. In 1949 India declared the continuation of full Commonwealth membership and accepted the Crown as head of the Commonwealth, an extra-constitutional declaration that does not affect sovereignty. Nehru told the Assembly in 1949 that a nation does not lose independence by an alliance, that the Commonwealth's strength is its flexibility and freedom, that any member may leave, and that it is an agreement by free will to be terminated by free will. India became a UN member in 1945 and this does not limit sovereignty. A sovereign India can acquire or cede territory.
concepts.example: Nehru said membership in the Commonwealth is an agreement by free will, to be terminated by free will.

concepts.name: Socialism in detail: Avadi, democratic socialism and case law
concepts.description: The Avadi resolution, Indira Gandhi's view, the Supreme Court's description and the effect of 1991.
concepts.idea: India's socialism is democratic, a mixed economy blending Marxism and Gandhism, and diluted after 1991.
concepts.rule: Before 1976 the Constitution had socialist content in some Directive Principles. The Congress at its Avadi session in 1955 resolved to establish a 'socialistic pattern of society', where principal means of production are under social ownership or control, production is progressively speeded up and national wealth is distributed equitably. Indira Gandhi said India has 'its own brand of socialism' and just nationalisation is not its type. Democratic socialism aims to end poverty, ignorance, disease and inequality of opportunity (G.B. Pant University case, 2000) and Indian socialism is a blend of Marxism and Gandhism leaning towards Gandhian socialism (Nakara case, 1982). It differs from communistic or state socialism, which nationalises all means of production and abolishes private property. The New Economic Policy of 1991 (liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation) diluted the socialist credentials.

concepts.name: Secularism in detail: types of state and definitions
concepts.description: Atheistic, theocratic and secular states and the descriptions by Gokhale and Gajendragadkar.
concepts.idea: A secular State is neutral in religion, unlike atheistic and theocratic states.
concepts.rule: On the basis of a state's attitude to religion three types can be conceived: the atheistic state, which is anti-religion and condemns all religions; the theocratic state, which is pro-religion and declares one religion the state religion, as in Bangladesh, Burma, Sri Lanka and Pakistan; and the secular state, neutral in religion and not upholding any religion as state religion, as in the USA and India. The Union Law Minister H.R. Gokhale said there will be freedom of faith and worship for all, and the State will treat every religion equally but have no foundation of religion. Former Chief Justice P.B. Gajendragadkar said the State does not owe loyalty to any religion, is not irreligious or anti-religious and gives equal freedom to all religions. The Indian Constitution embodies positive secularism, and it abolished communal representation but allows temporary reservation for SCs and STs.
concepts.example: P.B. Gajendragadkar was a former Chief Justice of India.

concepts.name: Democracy in detail: Greek origin, devices and Ambedkar's warning
concepts.description: The word democracy, the four devices of direct democracy defined, and the social democracy argument.
concepts.idea: Direct democracy uses referendum, initiative, recall and plebiscite, and social democracy underpins political democracy.
concepts.rule: Democracy comes from demos (people) and kratia (rule). A referendum refers proposed legislation to the electorate for settlement by direct vote. An initiative lets the people propose a bill to the legislature. A recall lets voters remove a representative or officer before the term ends when he fails in his duty. A plebiscite obtains the opinion of the people on an important issue and is generally used to settle territorial disputes. In his concluding speech on 25 November 1949 Ambedkar said political democracy cannot last unless social democracy lies at its base, meaning a way of life recognising liberty, equality and fraternity as a trinity; without equality liberty gives supremacy to the few, and equality without liberty kills initiative. In 1997 the Supreme Court said the Constitution envisions an egalitarian social order giving every citizen social, economic and political justice in a social and economic democracy.
concepts.example: A plebiscite is generally used to solve territorial disputes.

concepts.name: Tributes to the Preamble and its expert descriptions
concepts.description: The persons and phrases that describe the Preamble.
concepts.idea: Experts have called the Preamble the soul, key-note, horoscope and identity card of the Constitution.
concepts.rule: Alladi Krishnaswami Iyer: 'The Preamble to our Constitution expresses what we had thought or dreamt so long.' K.M. Munshi: the 'horoscope of our sovereign democratic republic'. Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava: 'the most precious part of the Constitution, the soul, a key, a jewel set in the Constitution and a proper yardstick with which one can measure the worth of the Constitution'. Sir Ernest Barker called it the 'key-note' to the Constitution, stated in a brief and pithy form the argument of much of his book, and he quoted it at the opening of Principles of Social and Political Theory (1951). M. Hidayatullah said it resembles the American Declaration of Independence but is more than a declaration and is the soul of the Constitution containing a solemn resolve which nothing but a revolution can alter. N.A. Palkhivala called it the identity card of the Constitution.
concepts.example: Ernest Barker quoted the Preamble at the opening of his book.

concepts.name: The Berubari, Kesavananda Bharati and LIC cases on the Preamble
concepts.description: The Article 143 reference on Berubari, and how the Court's view of the Preamble changed.
concepts.idea: The Court moved from saying the Preamble is not part of the Constitution to holding it is an integral part.
concepts.rule: The Berubari Union reference (1960) was made by the President under Article 143 on implementing the 1958 Indo-Pakistan agreement about the Berubari Union and exchange of enclaves. The Supreme Court said the Preamble shows the general purposes behind the provisions and is a key to the minds of the makers, and that ambiguity in an Article may be resolved with help from it, yet said it is not a part of the Constitution. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Court rejected that and held the Preamble is a part of the Constitution, to be read in light of its grand and noble vision. In LIC of India v. Consumer Education and Research Centre (1995) it again held the Preamble an integral part. The Preamble was enacted last. The President of the Assembly asked whether the Preamble stands part of the Constitution, and the motion was adopted. It is neither a source of power to the legislature nor a prohibition on its powers, and is non-justiciable. The Court in Kesavananda said the edifice of the Constitution rests on basic elements mentioned in the Preamble and removing them would change its identity.
concepts.example: The Berubari reference was made under Article 143.
